1. A 47-year-old male underwent L4-5 posterior lumbar decompression and fusion with instrumentation.
2. During the six-week clinical visit, he complains of pain in the region of his wound.
3. On physical exam, there is wound erythema but no exudate.
4. Laboratory studies show an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 78 mm/h (normal up to 20 mm/h) and WBC count of 11,200/mm3 (normal 3,500 to 10,500/mm3).
5. An MRI is performed and shows a fluid collection dorsal to the thecal sac.

1. Patient D is a 55-year-old  male who is post-op day 4 status-post C3-C5 anterior cervical discectomy and fusion
2. Patient D had some difficulty swallowing on post op day 1 which has improved and he is now able to take solid medications
3. In addition, he states that his arm pains have improved, but he continues to have significant surgical site pain and residual arm pain not relieved by acetaminophen
4. On physical examination, you find that his neck remains tender to palpation and he continues to have dysesthesias in both arms
5. The medication administration record indicates that he has been taking 1 dose of oxycodone every 6 hours for pain control.

1. A woman in her 70s was referred to our tertiary care center for an asymptomatic mass of the gastric fundus.
2. Her medical history was significant for chronic gastritis, which was being treated with esomeprazole 20 mg; a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 18 years prior; and excision of a 26-mm Merkel cell carcinoma of the left knee with negative results of the sentinel lymph node biopsy (stage II) 19 months prior.
3. Results of the patient’s follow-up examinations were negative until a high-resolution computed tomographic scan showed a 45 × 40-mm intraluminal protruding mass with slightly enlarged lymph nodes along the lesser curvature of the gastric fundus (Figure, A).
4. Results of fluorine 18–labeled fluorodeoxyglucose and gallium citrate Ga 68–labeled 1,4,7,10-tetraazacyclododecane-N,N',N'',N'''-tetraacetic (DOTA)-D-Phe1-Try3-octreotide (DOTATOC) positron emission tomography confirmed the presence of a metabolically active mass in the gastric fundus (maximum standardized uptake value, 6) with intense 68Ga–DOTATOC uptake (maximum standardized uptake value, 24) as well as mild 68Ga–DOTATOC uptake in 2 lymph nodes of the lesser curvature.A, Multislice computed tomographic scan showing the 45 × 40-mm mass in the gastric fundus.
5. B, Endoscopic image showing the endophytic lesion in the posterior wall of the gastric fundus at the esophagogastric junction.Preoperative workup was completed via esophagogastroduodenoscopy, which showed the presence of the polypoid lesion in the posterior wall of the gastric fundus at the level of the esophagogastric junction (Figure, B).
6. Multiple biopsies were performed at the time of the endoscopy.

1. An 18-month-old boy is brought to the emergency department in October due to a 1-day history of wheezing.  
2. His mother reports that he has had a runny nose and occasional dry cough for the past 3 days but has been otherwise healthy and feeding well.  
3. He was born at 38 weeks' gestation after an uncomplicated pregnancy and has no significant medical history.  
4. His immunizations are up-to-date.  
5. His temperature is 38°C (100.4°F), pulse is 135/min, respirations are 35/min, and blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg.  
6. Oxygen saturation on room air is 93%, and capillary refill time is 1 second.  
7. Lung examination reveals scattered rhonchi and end-expiratory wheezing bilaterally.  
8. No other abnormalities are noted.

1. A 25-year-old woman who is 19 weeks pregnant comes to the office for a prenatal examination.  
2. Her father had classic hemophilia.  
3. A karyotype obtained from an amniotic fluid sample of the patient shows that the fetus is XY.

1. A 44-year-old man with a history of gastroesophageal reflux disease and anxiety presents for evaluation of mouth ulcers recurring for the past 2 years.
2. The painful ulcers resolve within 2 weeks but recur on different mucosal surfaces.
3. He denies new medications, foods, or oral hygiene products and involvement of cutaneous or other mucosal surfaces.
4. He is uncertain whether he has a family history of oral ulcers.
5. He was previously prescribed anesthetic rinses and fluconazole, without benefit.
6. His current medications include omeprazole and lorazepam.
7. Intraoral examination demonstrates an ulcer with a pseudomembrane and erythematous halo on the left lateral surface of the tongue (Figure).
8. Physical examination results are otherwise normal.

1. A 41-year-old man presents to his primary care provider with a 2-month history of abdominal pain.
2. He says that the pain “comes and goes” throughout the day and usually lasts 20-30 minutes per episode.
3. The pain is above his umbilicus.
4. He denies any feeling of regurgitation or nighttime cough but endorses nausea.
5. He used to eat 3 large meals per day but has found that eating smaller meals more frequently improves his pain.
6. He tried ibuprofen with food and thinks it helped.
7. He has gained 4 pounds since his last appointment 3 months ago.
8. He denies any diarrhea or change in his stools.
9. He has no known medical history.
10. He drinks 5-6 beers on the weekend and has a 20 pack-year smoking history.
11. He denies any family history of cancer.
12. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 117/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 13/min.
13. On physical exam, he is tender to palpation above the umbilicus.
14. Bowel sounds are present.
15. A stool guaiac test is positive.
16. The patient undergoes an endoscopy with a biopsy to diagnose his condition.

1. A 64-year-old woman presented with a 6-month history of progressive bilateral proptosis and conjunctival erythema.
2. Her medical history was significant for hypothyroidism, treated with levothyroxine, as well as 2 forms of hematologic malignancy: retroperitoneal extranodal marginal zone lymphoma and indolent-phase T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia.
3. She had received no treatment for her hematologic malignancies, as she had been asymptomatic since her diagnoses 6 years prior.
4. Ophthalmological examination revealed 27 mm of bilateral proptosis, conjunctival injection, chemosis, and bilateral lower eyelid retraction (Figure 1A).
5. Visual acuity, color vision, and pupillary responses were normal.
6. Extraocular motility was full in all positions of gaze, and there was no associated pain.
7. Upper eyelid retraction was minimal.
8. Von Graefe sign (delayed descent of the upper eyelid with initiation of downgaze) and lagophthalmos were absent.
9. Results of slitlamp examination and dilated fundus examination were normal, including the appearance of both optic nerves.
10. A, Clinical photograph at presentation; bilateral proptosis, lower eyelid retraction, chemosis, and conjunctival injection are present.
11. There is mild temporal retraction of both upper eyelids.
12. B, Radiographic images documenting marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles bilaterally.
13. The lateral rectus is especially enlarged on both sides.
14. Using a measurement technique described by Dagi and colleagues, the maximal diameter of each extraocular muscle in this patient was as follows: right inferior rectus, 8.0 mm; right medial rectus, 9.1 mm; right superior muscle group, 9.7 mm; right lateral rectus, 9.3 mm; left inferior rectus, 8.1 mm; left medial rectus, 9.5 mm; left superior muscle group, 10.0 mm; and left lateral rectus, 9.6 mm.
15. There is sparing of anterior tendinous insertions (arrowheads) of each medial rectus (MR) and lateral rectus (LR).
16. However, the anterior portion of the muscle belly (brackets) appears uninvolved compared with the posterior portion, causing an acute taper of the muscle that is similar in shape to an amphora (inset).
17. An orbital computed tomography scan revealed marked enlargement of all extraocular muscles (Figure 1B).
18. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, and thyroid peroxidase antibody levels were normal.
19. Test results for autoimmune diseases, including sarcoidosis, Sjogren syndrome, granulomatous polyangiitis, IgG4 disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, and vasculitis, were negative.

1. An African American man in his 40s was referred for evaluation of a 3-week history of pain and swelling over his right orbit and upper eyelid.
2. Worsening edema prompted his primary care physician to initiate a course of oral methylprednisolone and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, which did not alleviate the symptoms.
3. Because of persistent swelling, he was referred for further evaluation.
4. The patient denied fevers, chills, purulent drainage, otalgia, or odynophagia.
5. The patient had no history of frequent sinusitis, trauma, or exposure to chemicals, but he did note poor dentition.
6. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS.
7. Pupils were reactive, extraocular motility was full, and intraocular pressure was 19 mm Hg OD and 16 mm Hg OS.
8. Exophthalmometer readings were 21 mm OD and 18 mm OS with a base of 120 mm.
9. Inspection of the right upper eyelid was remarkable for a 2.2-cm fluctuant mass with surrounding erythema that was tender to palpation.
10. Computed tomography (CT) of the face and head demonstrated a right supraorbital abscess with mass effect resulting in right hypoglobus, multiple communicating channels through inner and outer tables with cortical breakthrough in the frontal sinus, and advanced dental caries that communicated directly with the maxillary sinus owing to cortex erosion (Figure).
11. Coronal sections of a computed tomographic image of the orbits with intravenous contrast.
12. There is a 2.2-cm right supraorbital abscess with mass effect on the right globe leading to a hypoglobus (arrowhead).
13. The abscess has a direct communication with the right frontal sinus.
14. One of the channels that directly communicates with the right supraorbital abscess shows adjacent cortical breakthrough.
15. Of note, there are also extensive dental caries with direct erosion of the maxillary roots into the maxillary sinus.

1. A 44-year-old man presents to the emergency department with palpitations.
2. He has a history of anxiety managed with fluoxetine and lorazepam.
3. He also has hypertension but does not take any medications.
4. Today, his symptoms have been persistent despite taking his medications.
5. He says that he feels lightheaded and can’t walk.
6. His temperature is 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 120/72 mmHg, pulse is 183/min, respirations are 25/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air.
7. Physical exam reveals a somnolent and uncomfortable man.
8. His pulse is rapid and regular.
9. An ECG is performed as seen in Figure A.
10. During the exam, the patient states that he feels lightheaded and appears occasionally somnolent.

1. A man in his 30s presented with a 3-month history of gradual growth of a pruriginous, reddish nodule on the left ear.
2. He had no relevant medical history.
3. On medical examination, a reddish, smooth, superficial nodule with small dimples and a soft consistency that measured approximately 1.5 cm in diameter was seen on the left earlobe (Figure, A).
4. It was not painful to the touch.
5. The patient reported no history of lesions or foreign bodies at this location.
6. A biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B and C).
7. A, Clinical photograph of a pruriginous, reddish tumor on the earlobe.
8. B and C, Histopathologic findings reveal mixed diffuse dermatitis involving the reticular dermis, with small-vessel vasculitis, characteristic sparing of a superficial dermal grenz zone as well as the dilated vessel luminal, and mixed leukocytic infiltrate with eosinophils, lymphocytes, and neutrophils involving the full thickness of the vessel wall (hematoxylin-eosin).

1. A 42-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of persistent muscle twitching in his abdomen and bilateral calves during wakefulness and sleep accompanied with excessive sweating, as well as mild bilateral lower extremity weakness after prolonged walking.
2. The patient denied confusion, memory problems, hallucinations, and sleep disturbance.
3. He had psoriasis for 30 years, for which he was taking steroids intermittently, and hypothyroidism for 4 years, for which he was taking levothyroxine.
4. His family history was unremarkable.
5. His examination results were significant for psoriatic skin lesions and purple stria in the abdomen and both calves.
6. Undulating wavelike movements were visible on the muscle surface of the abdomen and calves (Video).
7. The remaining general and neurological examination results were normal.
8. Laboratory test results, including creatine kinase, thyrotropin, antinuclear antibodies, paraneoplastic antibodies (includes Hu, Yo, Ri, CV2, Ma2, and amphiphysin antibodies), were normal.
9. Chest computed tomography results were normal.

1. Patient D is a 60-year-old  female with history of prior L5-S1 posterior lumbar fusion who presents with 8 months of new thigh pain
2. Patient D states that she was previously in good health and pain-free since her last surgery, but for the last 8 months, she has had progressive discomfort in her anterior thighs
3. This discomfort has transformed into severe pain in the last 3 months, which she says is worse after prolonged ambulation and often keeps her from sleeping
4. When you examine Patient D, you discover bilateral hip flexor weakness and diminished sensation over her anterior thighs and knees
5. MRI and CT of the lumbar spine show intact instrumentation at L5-S1, but with new degenerative changes at L4-L5 resulting in canal and neuroforaminal stenosis
6. The findings are consistent with adjacent-level disease
7.

1. A 45-year-old woman was referred to the medical retina service for evaluation of bilateral macular atrophy noted by her general ophthalmologist.
2. Medical history was positive for bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with cochlear origin as determined by an otolaryngologist and headache since age 35 years.
3. She had no history of longer-term use of medications.
4. There was no family history of hearing and vision loss in all immediate family members.
5. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/63 OS.
6. Her pupils were round and reactive.
7. The anterior segment was unremarkable.
8. Fundus examination confirmed the presence of bilateral macular atrophy.
9. Fundus autofluorescence revealed a fairly symmetric loss of autofluorescence in the macula and in the regions surrounding the optic disc (Figure).
10. In proximity of these areas of reduced autofluorescence, a speckled fundus autofluorescence pattern of alternating spots of increased and decreased autofluorescence was also noted.
11. Optical coherence tomography displayed the presence of a bilateral atrophy of the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (Figure).
12. The patient’s family underwent a complete ophthalmologic evaluation, which did not display any alteration.A, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrates an area of pallor in the fundus (blue arrowheads) corresponding to the region of macular atrophy.
13. B, Structural optical coherence tomography (inset image) and green fundus autofluorescence (main image) of the right eye show a macular atrophy that also involves the peripapillary region.
14. The area of retinal pigment epithelium loss is featured by well-demarcated reduced autofluorescence (pink arrowhead) surrounded by speckled hyperautofluorescent areas (yellow arrowhead).
15. Structural optical coherence tomography confirms the presence of atrophy involving the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (red arrowheads in the inset image).Prescribe laboratory testing to investigate causes of intraocular inflammationGenetic testing to rule out a mitochondrial disease

1. A 45-year-old man visits his physician with complaints of increased urinary frequency and reduced urine volume over the past two months.
2. He denies experiencing pain during urination but feels frustrated about waking up two to three times nightly to urinate.
3. Efforts to reduce water intake before bed and make dietary changes have not improved his symptoms.
4. He has no family history of prostate conditions.
5. On physical examination, there is no evidence of a suprapubic mass or tenderness, and no costovertebral angle tenderness is noted.

1. A 33-year-old female is brought to emergency care after being discovered unconscious in her yard following alcohol intoxication and prolonged exposure to rain.
2. Her vital measurements show: temperature 31°C (87.8°F), heart rate 106/min, breathing rate 14/min, and blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg.
3. Clinical examination reveals pupil dilation, decreased reflexes, and general muscle rigidity.
4. Her ECG demonstrates J point elevation.

1. A 72-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit for pain management and observation of ventricular ectopy 4 hours after undergoing uncomplicated left total knee replacement.
2. He is receiving fentanyl via systemic patient-controlled analgesic pump for pain management.
3. Medical history is remarkable for coronary artery disease, for which he takes atorvastatin, furosemide, carvedilol, lisinopril, and 81-mg aspirin.
4. Baseline echocardiogram showed an ejection fraction of 0.20.
5. Vital signs now are temperature 38.0°C (100.4°F), pulse 90/min, respirations 16/min, and blood pressure 130/90 mm Hg.
6. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 96%.
7. Physical examination discloses no unexpected abnormalities.

1. Patient D is a 66-year-old  female who presents with 3 months of low-back pain
2. The pain is primarily axial and is exacerbated by bending, twisting and heavy lifting
3. Patient D has tried managing this pain with NSAIDs and low impact exercises recommended by a physical therapist, but her pain continues to worsen
4. On physical exam, her lumbar spine is tender to palpation, but she has no focal neurologic deficits
5. On further questioning, she reveals that she has had intermittent fevers and night sweats ever since she was hospitalized for a kidney infection 5 months ago
6. You obtain an MRI with contrast of her lumbar spine which reveals L3-4 pathology consistent with discitis-osteomyelitis and psoas abscesses.

1. A 40-year-old male presents to the office with symptoms of odynophagia and gastroesophageal reflux.
2. He also says that he experienced hematemesis once last week.
3. Past medical history reveals AIDS, and his most recent CD4 count was 30 cells/mcL.
4. The patient's tilt test result and hemoglobin level are normal.
5. Rectal examination demonstrates brown stool that is positive for occult blood.

1. A man in his 40s with a history of sinusitis presented with a 2-month history of worsening pain and redness of the right eye and nasal congestion.  
2. He was previously diagnosed with conjunctivitis and treated empirically with artificial tears, ofloxacin drops (0.3%), and prednisolone acetate drops (1%) 4 times a day, without improvement.  
3. His visual acuity was 20/20 OD.  
4. Examination findings of the anterior segment of the right eye revealed a raised, nonmobile, engorged perilimbal nodule in the inferotemporal sclera that was tender to palpation and did not blanch with phenylephrine drops (2.5%) (Figure, A).  
5. The ultrasonogram demonstrated a noncystic, regular, dome-shaped lesion with medium to high reflectivity localized to the sclera without intraocular involvement (Figure, B).  
6. The remaining results of the right-eye examination and the entire left-eye examination were within the reference range.  
7. In addition, the patient had a right-sided intranasal mass.  
8. A, Slitlamp photograph of the patient’s right eye at presentation.  
9. B, Anterior segment ultrasonography of the right eye at presentation.  
10. Laboratory test results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers, with an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 38 mm/h (reference range, 0-20 mm/h) and a C-reactive protein level of 190 mg/L (reference range, 0.08-3.1 mg/L) (to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).  
11. Results of serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, angiotensin-converting enzyme, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption, rapid plasma reagin, and tuberculosis skin testing were within their reference ranges.  
12. Results of urine microscopy had 4+ red blood cells per high-power field.  
13. His blood urea nitrogen and creatinine levels were within their reference ranges.

1. A 3-year-old boy with no significant medical history is evaluated for dehydration and refusal to eat or drink.  
2. Seven days ago, he developed a fever of 38.9°C, which resolved within 2 days.  
3. As the fever resolved, the child’s mother noticed fluid-filled bumps on his tongue and in his mouth.  
4. The bumps have spread and seem to be causing pain.  
5. The child is currently afebrile with mild tachycardia for his age and a capillary refill of about 2 seconds.  
6. He has dry mucous membranes and halitosis.  
7. Many painful, shallow ulcerations are evident on his tongue, buccal mucosa, and gingiva with areas of crusting, and there is tender submandibular lymphadenopathy.  
8. The rest of his physical examination is unremarkable.

1. A 41-year-old man who had immigrated to the United States from Costa Rica 10 years prior presented with a 2-year history of tingling and pain in his hands and feet.  
2. He had no other symptoms and reported taking no medications.  
3. Findings on skin examination included near-complete loss of eyebrows and eyelashes, a scaly plaque on the right shin, and mild bilateral erythema of the earlobes, distal fingers, and toes (Figure).  
4. He also had right axillary and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy.  
5. Check rapid plasma reagin, thyroid-stimulating hormone level, and lead level.  
6. Empirically treat patient and close contacts with dapsone

1. A 68-year-old man presented with progressive right-sided facial numbness and weakness, vision changes, and headaches.
2. His symptoms began 5 years earlier with right temple numbness, which expanded to include the entire right face and mouth.
3. He then developed progressive right facial weakness with a droop, slurred speech, and eyelid ptosis.
4. Finally, binocular vertical and horizontal diplopia and periorbital headaches began.
5. Trials of gabapentin and steroids provided no relief.
6. His history was significant for a left cheek melanoma completely excised years prior, numerous cutaneous squamous and basal cell carcinomas of the bilateral head and neck removed without issue, type 2 diabetes, and hyperlipidemia.
7. His medications included metformin and simvastatin; he had no history of smoking or drinking.
8. On examination, he had right-sided ptosis and severe right facial weakness in a lower motor neuron pattern with temporal wasting.
9. The right pupil was fixed and dilated.
10. There was no afferent pupillary defect.
11. The left pupil was appropriately sized and reactive.
12. His right-sided vision was impaired (20/250) with blurriness.
13. Vertical and horizontal binocular diplopia was present.
14. Right extraocular movements were significantly limited in all directions and painful, and right-sided facial sensation was diminished to pinprick in all cranial nerve (CN) V distributions.
15. His speech was slightly slurred.
16. Left-sided extraocular movements were intact.
17. His left facial sensation was intact to pinprick, and his strength was without deficit.
18. There were no other neurological abnormalities.
19. Initial magnetic resonance images (MRIs) were unremarkable.
20. A biopsy of CN VII was nondiagnostic.
21. Hemoglobin A1c was 6.8%.
22. Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results.
23. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) studies showed mildly elevated protein values.
24. Figure 1 shows the MRI at presentation.

1. Patient D is a 52-year-old  female who presents to your clinic with complaints of low back and leg pain
2. Patient D’s pain started gradually several years ago, and she state that the pain has been more severe for several months
3. Patient D says that ibuprofen and other over the counter pain medicines have not helped
4. Patient D has also tried physical therapy
5. Patient D’s physical exam is remarkable for pain limitation of the bilateral lower extremities
6.  Patient D was recently diagnosed with moderate-severe lumbar spondylosis by a neurosurgeon, and was told that she would eventually require a spinal fusion
7. Patient D is considering surgery but she would like for the pain to be well controlled until she reaches a decision.

1. A 79-year-old female presents for evaluation of a two-month history of nonproductive cough, fatigue, dyspnea on mild exertion, and a 4.5-kg weight loss.
2. Her medical history includes congestive heart failure, hypertension, a 47 pack-year smoking history, and 50 years of employment as a seamstress in a textile factory.
3. She recently traveled to India.
4. Current medications include enalapril, digoxin, isosorbide, spironolactone, and metoprolol.
5. Physical examination reveals a thin woman with dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base.
6. Vital signs show temperature 37.0°C, pulse 90/min, respirations 25/min, blood pressure 110/70 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 94% on room air.
7. Chest x-ray demonstrates right-sided nodular pleural lesions with moderate pleural effusion.

1. A 75-year-old man comes to the clinic reporting low back pain that he describes as tight and muscular, originating in the buttocks area.
2. The pain worsens with prolonged sitting but does not radiate.
3. He reports no bowel or urinary incontinence.
4. Physical examination reveals limited hip flexion and abduction range of motion.
5. While straight leg raise testing is negative, the right piriformis muscle shows hypertonicity.
6. Upon palpation, the physician identifies a small, tense, edematous area within the right piriformis muscle belly that elicits localized pain without radiation.

1. A 59-year-old man presents accompanied by his wife with nausea and dizziness.
2. He is unsure when his symptoms started, but they have been affecting him for “a while.” It began as episodes of “unsteadiness” that progressed to a feeling of “spinning.” He cannot tell if his symptoms change with position but reports that if he does not lie down he will become nauseous.
3. He also has worsening hearing loss worse on his right side.
4. The patient’s medical history is significant for hypertension, alcohol use disorder, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
5. His medications include aspirin, amlodipine, and fluticasone-salmeterol.
6. He drinks a glass of red wine every night with dinner and smokes a cigar on the weekends.
7. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 135/91 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 12/min.
8. Examination shows delayed horizontal nystagmus.

1. A 46-year-old man presents with his wife to his primary care provider for depression and strange movements.
2. His wife reports that her husband has not been himself for the last 2 months.
3. Whereas he was previously outgoing and “the life of the party,” the patient is now irritable and withdrawn.
4. He is a partner at an accounting firm, but his colleagues are threatening to fire him if he continues to perform poorly at work.
5. The patient cannot explain the recent changes to his mood and tearfully admits he fears there is something seriously wrong with him.
6. His wife says that he is getting worse.
7. The patient’s medical history is significant for hypertension, for which he takes lisinopril.
8. His family history is unknown as he was adopted.
9. The patient met his mother once and never knew his father but was told he died in his 50s.
10. He drinks a few glasses of wine per week and has never smoked.
11. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 141/87 mmHg, pulse is 81/min, and respirations are 12/min.
12. On physical exam, the patient has a flat affect with a facial grimace and sudden jerky movements of his upper extremities.

1. A 2.5-year-old male is evaluated for constipation that began 6 months ago.
2. Previously, he had daily soft bowel movements, but now passes hard stools every 3-4 days with straining and occasional blood on toilet paper.
3. Despite 4 months of polyethylene glycol treatment, he continues having hard stools every 2-3 days with intermittent bloating.
4. His diet is diverse and includes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, meats, and 14 ounces of low-fat milk daily.
5. The patient was born full-term with normal meconium passage.
6. Family history includes paternal Crohn disease and type 1 diabetes in a maternal cousin.
7. Physical examination reveals a happy child with normal vital signs, though his weight has decreased from the 40th to 25th percentile over 4 months while maintaining height at the 45th percentile.
8. His abdomen is mildly distended with palpable stool in the left lower quadrant.
9. Digital rectal examination shows normal tone with hard stool present.
10. Neurological examination, including deep-tendon reflexes, is normal, and his back shows no abnormalities.

1. A 6-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling from his scooter.
2. He has dull, aching pain along his left side where he hit the ground.
3. He fell sideways off the scooter as he rounded a curve in the road.
4. He has never had any serious injuries but that he always seems to bruise easily, especially after he started playing soccer this fall.
5. His parents deny that he has an abnormal number of nosebleeds or bleeding from the gums.
6. They have never seen blood in his stool or urine.
7. His mother notes that her brother has had similar problems.
8. His temperature is 98.6°F (37°C), blood pressure is 112/74 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, and respirations are 11/min.
9. On physical exam, the patient has extensive bruising of the lateral left thigh and tenderness to palpation.

1. A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of numbness in her right hand.
2. During this period, she has had tingling in the right ring and small fingers most of the time.
3. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications.
4. She is employed as a cashier and uses a computer at home.
5. She played as a pitcher in a softball league for 5 years until she stopped 2 years ago.
6. Vital signs are within normal limits.
7. Examination shows full muscle strength.
8. Palpation of the right elbow produces a jolt of severe pain in the right ring and small fingers.
9. Sensation to pinprick and light touch is decreased over the medial half of the right ring finger and the entire small finger.

1. A 51-year-old man presents to his primary care provider for intermittent shaking of his hands.
2. For the last several years he has noticed this "shaking" when he brushes his teeth and prepares a cup of coffee in the morning.
3. The shaking then gradually improves over the course of the day.
4. His medical history is otherwise notable for hypertension and hyperlipidemia.
5. His only home medication is pravastatin.
6. The patient smokes half a pack per day of cigarettes and drinks 2-3 beers throughout the day.
7. His family history is significant for Parkinson disease in his father.
8. On physical exam, his temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 159/84, pulse is 74/min, and respirations are 12/min.
9. He has a high-frequency bilateral hand tremor elicited on finger-to-nose testing.
10. His neurological exam is otherwise unremarkable.

1. Patient D is a 60-year-old  male with history of prior L5-S1 posterior lumbar fusion who presents with 8 months of new thigh pain
2. Patient D states that he was previously in good health and pain-free since his last surgery, but for the last 8 months, he has had progressive discomfort in his anterior thighs
3. This discomfort has transformed into severe pain in the last 3 months, which he says is worse after prolonged ambulation and often keeps his from sleeping
4. When you examine Patient D, you discover bilateral hip flexor weakness and diminished sensation over his anterior thighs and knees
5. MRI and CT of the lumbar spine show intact instrumentation at L5-S1, but with new degenerative changes at L4-L5 resulting in canal and neuroforaminal stenosis
6. The findings are consistent with adjacent-level disease
7.

1. A 55-year-old man who is a business executive is admitted to the hospital for evaluation of abdominal pain.  
2. He is polite to the physician but berates the nurses and other staff.  
3. The patient's wife and two of his three adult children arrive for a visit.  
4. The patient says with disgust that the missing child is and always has been worthless.

1. A 53-year-old man presents to the clinic with a non-tender mass in his right anterior neck.
2. The mass has been slowly enlarging over the past 1 year.
3. He reports no dysphagia, difficulty breathing, or changes to his voice.
4. He also denies heat intolerance, palpitations, tremors, or diarrhea.

1. A 70-year old man with a history of soft contact lens wear presented for a general eye examination.

3. Routine laboratory studies reveal a leukocyte count of 25.0 × 103/mcL (reference range 4.5-11.0 × 103/mcL) and 97% mature-appearing lymphocytes on a peripheral blood smear.
4. Immunohistochemical stains demonstrate the lymphocytes to be of B-cell origin.

1. A 63-year-old woman is in the hospital recovery room 4 hours after elective left hemicolectomy for colon carcinoma at the splenic flexure.  
2. She has a preoperative written directive for no blood products through transfusion for religious reasons.  
3. Medical history is significant for hypertension and coronary artery disease.  
4. The nurse tells you the patient's blood pressure has progressively declined since the operation.  
5. Vital signs now are temperature 35.8°C (96.4°F), pulse 130/min, respirations 20/min, and blood pressure 80/50 mm Hg.  
6. Physical examination discloses a slightly distended abdomen with an intact incision.  
7. ECG shows sinus tachycardia.  
8. Urine output has been 10 mL during the past 2 hours.  
9. Hematocrit is 30%; preoperative hematocrit was 41%.  
10. The patient has received 4 L of intravenous crystalloid in the recovery room.  
11. Reported operative blood loss was 200 mL.  
12. Drainage from the nasogastric tube is clear.

1. A 58-year-old overweight African American man presented with a 5-year history of a slightly pruritic and painful rash of the right lateral area of the neck and right axilla.
2. It was worse during the summers, and blisters sometimes developed.
3. Emollients were unhelpful.
4. The patient was otherwise healthy.
5. His sister had diabetes mellitus and a similar rash in her axillae.
6. The patient performed indoor manual labor as a maintenance engineer and had no significant sun exposure.
7. Physical examination revealed irregularly thickened skin of the right axilla (Figure 1, left) and right lateral area of the neck (Figure 1, right) containing hyperpigmentation, hypopigmentation, multiple acrochordons (skin tags), malodorous crust, and areas of maceration and erosion.
8. Further examination of the skin revealed pseudofolliculitis barbae in the submental and mandibular regions bilaterally.
9. The nails, oral cavity, and mucosal membranes appeared normal.
10. A biopsy of right axillary skin was performed (Figure 2).Left, Rash of right axilla.
11. Right, Rash of right lateral area of the neck with global view and close-up view (inset).Epidermal acantholysis causing separation of keratinocytes into dilapidated brick wall appearance (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×10).

1. A man in his early 30s presented with 4 days of acute, monocular, painless vision loss.  
2. His visual acuity was 20/200 OD and 20/20 OS.  
3. There was no afferent pupillary defect, his color vision was intact bilaterally, and his intraocular pressures were normal.  
4. No anterior chamber or vitreal inflammation was present.  
5. Ophthalmoscopic examination of the right macula revealed a 2–disc diameter area of heterogeneous yellow retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) discoloration with overlying neurosensory retinal detachment and several small retinal hemorrhages (Figure 1A).  
6. The optic disc and retinal vessels were unremarkable, and ophthalmoscopic examination of the left eye revealed no abnormalities.A, Fundus photography of the right eye shows retinal pigment epithelial discoloration and retinal hemorrhages.  
7. B, Optical coherence tomography demonstrates neurosensory retinal detachment overlying irregular retinal pigment epithelium and thickened choroid.The patient denied recent corticosteroid use, joint pain, weight loss, myalgias, or cardiovascular, neurologic, or gastrointestinal symptoms.  
8. He had fevers and mild upper respiratory tract symptoms 2 weeks before his presentation, closely followed by a rash on his hands and thighs.  
9. A young family member had similar symptoms.Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) revealed a fovea-involving neurosensory retinal detachment, outer photoreceptor thickening, and an intact external limiting membrane overlying a zone of mildly thickened, irregular RPE.  
10. The submacular choroid was relatively thick bilaterally on enhanced depth imaging OCT (Figure 1B).  
11. Combined fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography demonstrated mottled early hyperfluorescence with late staining and minimal pooling.  
12. There was no leakage from the retinal vessels or optic discs bilaterally, and uninvolved areas of RPE and choroidal vasculature were unremarkable.  
13. A test for rapid plasma reagin was negative.Observe; follow up in 4 to 6 weeks with SD-OCTTreat with intravitreal antivascular endothelial growth factor injection

1. A 35-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 3-day history of severe right back pain.  
2. She has not had any fever, chills, or weight loss.  
3. She has no history of major medical illness.  
4. Musculoskeletal and neurologic examinations show no abnormalities.  
5. When told that her examination is normal, the patient becomes tearful and demands an MRI of her back because her mother just died from breast cancer metastatic to bone and she fears that she may also have cancer.  
6. The patient already contacted her insurance company, who told her that if she has neurologic abnormalities an MRI may be covered by her plan.  
7. The patient asks the physician to order the MRI indicating that she has neurologic findings.

1. A 76-year-old man was referred to an oculoplastic surgeon for evaluation of trichiasis.
2. The patient complained of 6 months of worsening tearing and crusting of both eyes that was worse on the left.
3. Three weeks before the evaluation, he was seen by his primary ophthalmologist, who epilated 2 misdirected eyelashes of the patient’s left lower eyelid and recommended eyelid scrubs and artificial tears.
4. The patient tried this treatment, but his symptoms did not improve.
5. His ocular history was significant for cataracts, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and macular degeneration.
6. He had a medical history of basal cell carcinoma of his left cheek and brow, both removed several years previously.
7. His medical history also included type 2 diabetes with diabetic neuropathy.
8. Slitlamp examination revealed bilateral meibomian gland dysfunction with upper and lower eyelid laxity, scurf, and collarettes.
9. There was a 6.5-mm area of left lower eyelid margin thinning associated with surrounding misdirected eyelashes and central madarosis, as well as meibomian orifice effacement and overlying telangiectatic vessels (Figure 1) without entropion.
10. External photograph shows left lower eyelid margin thinning, misdirected eyelashes, and central madarosis with meibomian gland orifice effacement and telangiectasias.
11. Epilate the misdirected lashes and return in 3 months

1. A 64-year-old man was referred to our clinic for suspected central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) in his right eye.
2. He had experienced blurred vision of the right eye for 2 months; medical history included hypercholesterolemia.
3. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS.
4. The anterior segment was normal and intraocular pressure was 16 mm Hg in both eyes.
5. Dilated fundus examination of the right eye revealed a normal optic disc, mild venous engorgement, and widespread peripheral dot-blot retinal hemorrhages mainly located in the temporal midperiphery (Figure 1A).
6. No spontaneous retinal arterial pulsation was noted.
7. Examination findings of the left eye were unremarkable.
8. Fluorescein angiography in the right eye showed delayed venous filling, mild perifoveal leakage, and scattered microaneurysms in the temporal sector (Figure 1B).
9. A, Montage color fundus photograph of the right eye at presentation shows mild venous dilation and midperipheral dot and blot hemorrhages mostly located in the temporal sectors.
10. B, Fluorescein angiography frame (2 minutes, 3 seconds) shows multiple microaneurysms in correspondence of the dot-blot retinal hemorrhages and a barely visible perifoveal vascular leakage.

1. A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back, accompanied by shortness of breath and pain with swallowing.
2. The symptoms began 30 minutes ago following heavy alcohol consumption and repeated episodes of forceful vomiting.
3. His medical history includes hypertension, alcohol use disorder, and liver cirrhosis.
4. On examination, his temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), blood pressure is 142/78 mmHg, and pulse is 75/min.
5. Crepitus is noted on palpation of the upper chest wall, and abdominal examination reveals hepatosplenomegaly.

1. A 27-year-old male presents to the emergency department with acute palpitations, sweating, and tremor.
2. His vital signs show a heart rate of 105/min, blood pressure 142/82 mm Hg, and temperature 37.2°C.
3. Initial glucometer reading is 40 mg/dL.
4. Laboratory results after IV placement show:

|  | Patient value | Reference range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glucose (mg/dL) | 55 | 70–100 |
| Insulin (μU/mL) | 25 | 2–20 |
| C-peptide (ng/mL) | 2.9 | 0.5–2.0 |

His symptoms resolve after oral administration of 20g glucose, with glucose rising to 78 mg/dL.
5. The patient's BMI is 28.1 (90 kg, 179 cm), and he underwent gastric bypass surgery 14 months ago, having previously weighed 141 kg with prediabetes.
6. He reports similar episodes occurring within hours after meals over the past few months, with the current episode beginning 3 hours after consuming corn, chicken breast, and a banana.
7. He has no history of smoking, alcohol use, or family diabetes.

1. A 24-year-old man with epilepsy refractory to valproic acid, phenytoin, and levetiracetam undergoes magnetic resonance imaging of his brain while monitored by anesthetic care.
2. He wakes up screaming in pain due to an electrocardiogram lead having caused a significant thermal burn circumferentially around his left leg.
3. He is admitted to the medical intensive care unit for continuous electroencephalogram monitoring while on a midazolam infusion for seizure suppression and supportive care for his burn.
4. Overnight, the nurse continued to increase the patient's midazolam infusion rate, but she also noticed that his left toes were cold to the touch with significant edema.
5. His temperature is now 100°F (37.8°C), blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg, pulse is 80/min, respirations are 10/min and oxygen saturation is 95% on 2 liters nasal cannula.
6. No dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulses are detected on the left lower extremity.
7. A delta pressure of 25 mmHg is obtained in the left leg.

1. A 26-year-old male police officer comes to the office for an annual health maintenance examination.
2. He is physically active and feels well, but he notes that his asthma has been more active during the past month.
3. He says that he has had to use his albuterol inhaler one to two times daily for wheezing and chest tightness.
4. He has not had gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, productive cough, or fever.
5. Medical history is remarkable for atopic allergies, especially to pollen and cats.
6. He has had coldand exercise-induced asthma for the past 14 years.
7. He takes no other medications.
8. He is 188 cm (6 ft 2 in) tall and weighs 90 kg (200 lb); BMI is 25 kg/m2 .
9. Vital signs are temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse 70/min, respirations 12/min, and blood pressure 120/76 mm Hg.
10. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for scattered rhonchi and wheezes with forced expiration.
11. Peak expiratory flow rate is 240 L/min.

1. An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office by his mother because of a 3-day history of fever, sore throat, and itchy eyes.  
2. He just returned from a weeklong summer camp that included hiking trips and swimming lessons in the camp-owned swimming pool.  
3. He has no history of major medical illness and receives no medications.  
4. He appears tired.  
5. His temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F); other vital signs are within normal limits.  
6. Physical examination shows conjunctival injection and discharge and oropharyngeal erythema.  
7. The public health department reports an outbreak of similar symptoms among the other campers and camp volunteers.

1. A 43-year-old man presented as a referral for bilateral central vision loss.
2. His medical history was significant for Crohn disease controlled with monthly injections of ustekinumab (Stelara; Janssen Biotech Inc).
3. Symptoms of fever, headache, and myalgia began 1 week prior following a tick bite.
4. He was prescribed oral doxycycline hyclate for suspected Lyme disease.
5. Owing to persistent fever while receiving oral doxycycline hyclate, he was admitted for intravenous administration of doxycycline hyclate, and the fever resolved.
6. He was found to be anemic (hemoglobin concentration, 6.7 g/dL; normal concentration, 13.5-17.5 g/dL) (to convert hemoglobin concentration to g/L, multiply by 10), requiring transfusion.
7. While hospitalized, he developed acute bilateral central scotoma.
8. Magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit and brain with and without contrast was unremarkable.
9. Infectious serology test results for Lyme disease, syphilis, malaria, Anaplasma species, Cryptococcus species, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and rickettsia were negative.
10. Rheumatologic serology test results for antinuclear antibodies, including Sjögren anti-Ro and anti-La, anti-DNA, and anti-Smith, were also negative.
11. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing revealed elevated proteinase 3 antibody level.
12. In the setting of anemia, infectious-disease consultants raised concern for babesiosis.
13. Peripheral blood smear and polymerase chain reaction were performed; empirical therapy of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, plus atovaquone, 750 mg twice daily, was initiated.
14. Polymerase chain reaction results for babesiosis later returned as negative.Ocular examination revealed uncorrected distance acuity of 20/50 OD and 20/60 OS.
15. Intraocular pressure values were normal, and there was no afferent pupillary defect.
16. Slitlamp evaluation showed bilateral rare anterior vitreous cell.
17. Dilated fundus examination revealed bilateral reddened foveal lesions and irregular macular pigmentation.

1. A 22-year-old woman comes to the office because of urticaria.
2. This is her first episode of urticaria and it has occurred and then resolved several times in the past week.
3. The history and physical examination disclose no abnormalities.

1. An adolescent boy was referred to the emergency department for suspected herpes zoster infection by his pediatrician.
2. He presented with a 2-day history of painful, left-sided vesicular rash around his eyelid and forehead.
3. Medical history was significant for a heart murmur with no known history of chickenpox.
4. His pediatrician prescribed oral acyclovir and ibuprofen as needed for pain.
5. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/25-2 OS.
6. On examination, clear vesicles on erythematous bases were noted in the V1 distribution with left upper eyelid edema and erythema.
7. Pupils were equally reactive with no relative afferent pupillary defect.
8. Visual fields were full in both eyes.
9. Anterior examination was significant for left-sided conjunctivitis, dendritic keratitis (Figure), and anterior uveitis.
10. The findings of the remainder of the examination, including the anterior segment of the right eye and the dilated fundus examination of both eyes, were unremarkable.
11. Slitlamp photograph showing branching corneal pseudodendrites with minimal fluorescein uptake.

1. A 27-year-old female with no prior medical history presents to the clinic with tightness in her neck.  
2. The patient states that she started feeling the tightness immediately after a stretching exercise yesterday.  
3. On initial exam, the patient is in no acute distress.  
4. There is decreased range of motion of the neck and increased hypertonicity in the paraspinal muscles on the right from C2–C7.

1. A 4-year-old boy presented with a pink nodule on his left cheek.
2. The lesion started as a hyperpigmented macule 3 years ago and since then had been gradually increasing in size and developing into a pink nodule.
3. The lesion was pruritic at times and sometimes bled with minor trauma.
4. The boy was otherwise healthy, with an unremarkable medical history and with no history of trauma or exposure to radiation.
5. On physical examination, there was a 1-cm well-circumscribed, symmetrical, pinkish, dome-shaped nodule with central erosions on the left cheek (Figure 1).
6. Hair, nails, and mucosae were of normal appearance, and the remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

1. A female patient in her late 40s presented with a 3-year history of nonhealing ulcers in her groin and axillae.
2. These lesions started as itchy, weepy, reddish papules and plaques, which gradually progressed to form ulcers and were associated with pain and pus discharge.
3. They did not heal completely after multiple courses of topical as well as systemic antibiotics, antifungals, and steroids.
4. She frequently experienced scaling and greasiness on her scalp, which was treated with shampoos and topical steroids.
5. She also complained of polyuria and polydipsia for the past 4 years.
6. General examination revealed multiple mobile, firm, nonmatted, and nontender lymph nodes in cervical and inguinal region.
7. On systemic examination, hepatomegaly (2 cm below the right costal margin) was seen.
8. There was also bilateral enlargement of the parotid area, which was tender on palpation.
9. Cutaneous examination revealed yellowish greasy scales on the scalp, suggestive of seborrheic dermatitis.
10. Erythematous edematous papules were present over the retroauricular areas and the inframammary folds (Figure, A).
11. On examination of external genitalia, deep ulcers were observed in the bilateral inguinal folds, resembling knife-cut ulcers (Figure, B).
12. Similar lesions were present over the junction of labia majora and labia minora and were associated with yellowish pus discharge.
13. A 3.5-mm punch biopsy specimen was obtained for histopathological examination from the edge of an ulcer on one of the groin folds (Figure, C and D).
14. A, Erythematous and edematous papules in the inframammary area.
15. B, Deep ulcers in the groin folds resembling knife-cut ulcers with yellowish pus discharge.
16. C, Histopathological examination of the area with intact epidermis shows dense infiltration of the ulcer bed by atypical cells.
17. These cells were large and had characteristic grooved vesicular nuclei and moderate amphophilic cytoplasm.
18. D, Immunohistochemistry shows diffuse positivity for CD1a in the lower epidermis and dermis.

1. A man in his 20s presented with a 2-month history of vague, right upper-quadrant abdominal pain, with associated 5-kg weight loss, loss of appetite, and increasing abdominal distension.
2. He reported a small mass in the right scrotum that was evaluated 5 years previously and was reassured to be a nonmalignant lesion.
3. Physical examination was notable for a distended abdomen with a palpable left abdominal mass.
4. Testicular examination revealed an approximately 1-cm firm right spermatic cord nodule.
5. Laboratory tests showed lactate dehydrogenase levels of 818 U/L (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167), with no significant β-human chorionic gonadotropin and α-fetoprotein levels.
6. Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen (Figure, A and B) revealed innumerable masses throughout the abdomen and pelvis, with the largest measuring 17.5 × 14 × 14 cm and a 3.9-cm enhancing lesion in the left hepatic lobe, and a small amount of ascites.
7. Testicular sonogram disclosed a 1.5-cm right epididymal cyst.
8. Percutaneous biopsy and histologic examination of the dominant left abdominal mass revealed neoplastic cells (Figure, C) that were positive for cytokeratin, desmin but negative for S100.
9. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) was positive for EWS-WT1 rearrangement.A, Coronal view and B, sagittal view contrast-enhanced computed tomographic imaging revealed innumerable abdominopelvic masses.
10. Blue arrowheads indicate the dominant mass and the red arrowhead indicates the liver mass.
11. C, Hematoxylin-eosin stain (original magnification ×40).

1. You are visiting an 86-year-old woman in her home at the request of the patient's daughter because of worsening shortness of breath at rest for the past 2 days.
2. The patient is confined to her home because of severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with cor pulmonale.
3. She was discharged 1 week ago from the hospital following 3 weeks of treatment for pneumonia that required intubation; her hospital stay was complicated by sepsis.
4. She had a prolonged weaning program from intubation.
5. Prior to discharge, the patient and her daughter met with you to review the patient's advance directive.
6. During the discussion, the patient said, "I'd rather die than be intubated again." At that time, both the patient and her daughter signed an addendum to that effect on the patient's advance directive.
7. Today, the patient is dyspneic and is unable to complete a sentence.
8. Vital signs are temperature 37.8°C (100.0°F), pulse 88/min, respirations 35/min, and blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg.
9. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 84% while the patient is breathing 4 L of oxygen.
10. You ask the patient if she wishes to return to the hospital.
11. She says, "No, I want to die at home." Her daughter takes you aside and says, "My mother doesn't know what she's saying.

1. A 55-year-old woman with small cell carcinoma of the lung is admitted to the hospital to undergo chemotherapy.
2. Six days after treatment is started, she develops a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F).
3. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities.
4. Laboratory studies show a leukocyte count of 100/mm3 (5% segmented neutrophils and 95% lymphocytes).

1. A woman in her 60s presented with a 2-year history of an abnormal left second fingernail.
2. A previous biopsy showed a pyogenic granuloma, and she had been treated with curettage and electrodessication.
3. In the few months before presentation, she experienced partial nail loss and her nail had become painful with intermittent drainage.
4. Her medical history was significant for streptococcal glomerulonephritis and 2 prior kidney transplants.
5. Her medications included prednisone, tacrolimus, and mycophenolate mofetil.
6. Physical examination of the left second fingernail showed a tender ulcerated nodule encompassing the nail bed with near-complete nail loss and purulent drainage (Figure 1, left).
7. A nail biopsy was repeated by performing a 4-mm punch through the nail bed.
8. The specimen was analyzed by histopathology with hematoxylin-eosin staining and once again showed a pyogenic granuloma–like response characterized by proliferating blood vessels in a background of fibrosis and reactive plasmacytic infiltration (Figure 1, right).
9. Careful inspection of the pyogenic granulomatous process at higher power demonstrated atypical epithelioid and spindled cells adjacent to blood vessels.Left, Physical examination of left second fingernail.
10. Right, Histopathologic findings under low-power magnification (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20).

1. A healthy 36-year-old man was referred to the dermatology clinic for a 5-day history of an exquisitely tender rash at the base of his left thumb.
2. One day prior to presentation, he went to a local emergency department, where he was prescribed clindamycin and valacyclovir.
3. The patient works as a plumber and attributed his tender rash to a “spider bite” he had incurred while working in an old building.
4. The patient was afebrile, and physical examination revealed several vesicles with purulent fluid on an erythematous base, at the base of the left thumb (Figure).
5. There was no lymphadenopathy, lymphangitis, or mucous membrane involvement.
6. The rash was not found elsewhere on the body.
7. Vesicular fluid was collected and sent for further analysis.

1. A boy aged 17 years presented after noticing that his right pupil was off-center.  
2. He had a high hyperopic refractive error, and the magnification of his spectacle lenses highlighted the eccentric pupil.  
3. He had no associated symptoms of decreased vision, ocular pain, diplopia, glare, or haloes and had no history of ocular infection, surgical procedure, or trauma.  
4. His mother, also hyperopic, previously underwent prophylactic laser iridotomy for anatomically narrow, occludable angles.  
5. Best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 OU, with a manifest refraction of +7.75 −1.00 × 170 OD and +7.75 −1.25 × 010 OS.  
6. Slitlamp examination confirmed mild corectopia in the right eye, along with 4 clock hours of iridocorneal touch nasally and a “hammered silver” appearance to the involved cornea (Figure 1).  
7. On examination via gonioscopy, there were high peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS) above the Schwalbe line in this area, while the remaining angle was deep without PAS.  
8. The left eye was normal.  
9. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 14 mm Hg OS.  
10. Pachymetry testing revealed symmetric central corneal thicknesses of 577 μm OD and 582 μm OS.  
11. Both optic discs appeared healthy, with a cup-disc ratio of 0.2.  
12. There were no visual field defects.  
13. Slitlamp photography showed the right eye had mild corectopia and iridocorneal touch nasally.

1. A woman in her 50s presented with “speckled” red lesions on her bilateral arms, lower legs, and feet.
2. They had first appeared on her lower legs 15 years ago and were slowly increasing in number and spreading to involve her feet and bilateral upper extremities.
3. The patient denied tenderness, pruritus, and edema.
4. She reported no family history of this problem and denied any personal history of anemia, epistaxis, hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, or hemoptysis.
5. She had a medical history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and tobacco abuse, requiring treatment with losartan and atorvastatin.
6. Physical examination revealed punctate, blanchable telangiectasias coalescing to form large, retiform patches on her bilateral lower extremities, feet, and upper extremities (Figure, A).
7. There was no conjunctival or mucosal involvement.
8. The patient reported no dermatographism or purpura.
9. Histologic findings from a biopsy specimen are shown in the Figure, B.
10. A, Multiple telangiectasias coalescing to form large, retiform patches on the bilateral lower extremities.
11. B, Dilated, ectatic vessels in the superficial dermis with no associated inflammation or fibrinoid necrosis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×200).

1. A 48-year-old male patient reports experiencing recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and diarrhea over the past year.
2. He describes his stools as watery, frothy, and bulky, with some episodes occurring without associated abdominal pain.
3. Additionally, he mentions three episodes of intense flushing over his head and neck without an identifiable cause.
4. Physical examination reveals no significant abnormalities.
5. Further diagnostic evaluation confirms the presence of metastasized carcinoid tumors.
6. The physician discusses the condition with the patient and recommends long-term treatment with octreotide.

1. A 24-year-old G1P0000 woman attends her first prenatal visit at approximately 8 weeks of gestation.
2. She reports no significant symptoms other than increased fatigue and occasional nausea.
3. The patient recently immigrated from Africa and works as a babysitter for neighborhood children, one of whom recently had the flu and another with chickenpox.
4. She has no immunization records and does not recall receiving any vaccines.
5. She is sexually active only with her husband, has no history of sexually transmitted infections or intravenous drug use, and her husband has no medical issues.
6. Her temperature is 98.7°F (37.1°C), blood pressure is 122/76 mmHg, pulse is 66/min, and respirations are 12/min.
7. Physical examination is unremarkable.

1. A 3-year-old healthy girl is brought to the emergency department due to concerns about an abdominal mass.
2. Her parents report a 3-week history of abdominal pain, reduced appetite, and a progressively protuberant abdomen.
3. This morning, while bathing her, they felt a hard area beneath her ribs.
4. She has not experienced weight loss, fevers, or changes in bowel habits.
5. On examination, the child appears playful and well.
6. Vital signs include a heart rate of 97 beats per minute, blood pressure of 92/56 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 100% on room air.
7. Palpation reveals a firm, nontender mass in the right upper quadrant extending approximately 4 cm below the costal margin.
8. Her abdomen is distended but soft, and the remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable.
9. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel, are normal.

1. Patient D is a 55-year-old  female presenting with 9 months of progressive low-back and leg pain
2. Patient D states that her pain is worse after prolonged ambulation and radiates to her right buttock and thigh
3. The pain has become constant in the last 2 months and she is unable to function effectively at her job because of the pain
4. Patient D has tried physical therapy and conservative pain medications including epidural steroid injections and NSAIDs
5. On physical exam, you observe that her pain is significantly worse with a right straight-leg raise and there are no focal deficits
6. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals grade-2 spondylolisthesis at L4-L5 with degenerative changes contributing to severe canal and neuroforaminal stenosis
7. Flexion-extension X rays show dynamic instability of L4 on L5.

1. During a recent hiking trip, a 17-year-old girl with up-to-date immunizations stepped on a wire, which went through her sneaker and punctured her right heel.
2. She was prescribed a 5-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.
3. Seven days after completing the antibiotics, she is unable to bear weight on her right foot and reports purulent drainage from her right heel.

1. A 69-year-old man with a smoking history and complaints of back pain and cough for 2 weeks was found to have a right lung mass on chest radiography results.

3. A biopsy was performed, and the pathologic report showed a poorly differentiated lung adenocarcinoma with ROS1 rearrangement identified by immunohistochemical staining (clone: D4D6; H-score: 280) and further confirmative fluorescence in situ hybridization.
4. The patient received ceritinib, 450 mg/day, and his tumor and brain and bone metastatic lesions subsequently decreased in size.
5. The ceritinib was then shifted to crizotinib, 500 mg/day, when the reimbursement of crizotinib as a first-line therapy was approved by Taiwan's National Health Insurance system.
6. Three weeks after the first dose of crizotinib, the patient developed a dry cough without fever or purulent sputum.
7. There was no significant finding on physical examination except mild crackles over the right lung field, although chest radiography results showed a new consolidation lesion over the right upper lobe.
8. Meanwhile, the results of mycobacterial and bacteriologic surveys were unremarkable.
9. The tumor marker carcinoembryonic antigen level decreased from an initial 14.76 to 0.71 ng/mL (reference range, 0-5.00 ng/mL [to convert to micrograms per liter, multiply by 1]).
10. A CT scan was arranged, and developing lung cancer with lymphangitic carcinomatosis was highly suspected by the radiologist (Figure, A).
11. A bronchoscopy with bronchial brushing and biopsy was performed, and no pathogen was identified.
12. A, The comparison of the chest computed tomographic (CT) scan of the new consolidation lesion (red arrowheads) mimicking recurrence (right panel) with the primary tumor (yellow arrowhead) in the initial CT scan (left panel).
13. B, Microscopic findings of a CT-guided biopsy (left panel) and CT scan after resuming ceritinib treatment (right panel).
14. Granulomatous inflammation or sarcoid-like reaction with predominant T-cell infiltration (hematoxylin and eosin stain, magnification ×200) and less B cell infiltration.
15. Inset: double immunohistochemical staining showing abundant T cells (CD3, red staining; red arrowheads) and rare B cell infiltration (CD20, brown staining; yellow arrowhead).
16. The CT scan after resuming ceritinib treatment for 2 months showed decreased lung consolidation and the primary tumor (yellow arrowhead).
17. Treat with chemotherapy for disease recurrence because the agents available for recurrent ROS1 tumors remain limited.
18. Administer antibiotics with coverage for pneumonia pathogen for 7 to 10 days and a repeated CT scan in 4 weeks.
19. Administer steroid treatment and discontinue crizotinib and other tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) permanently because TKI-induced interstitial lung disease is highly suspected.
20. Perform a CT-guided biopsy for histological confirmation of recurrence or identification of other benign disease, such as granulomatous inflammation

1. A 57-year-old male with atrial fibrillation on warfarin therapy is brought to the emergency department with altered mental status.

1. A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency room with a headache and nausea.

1. A 72-year-old woman was referred for an eye examination because of visual changes in the left eye.

1. A man in his 60s presented with a painless rapidly enlarging ulcer on his left leg 1 week after the onset of diverticulitis, a neutropenic fever, and severe sepsis due to multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection that necessitated admission to the intensive care unit.

7. A, Cutaneous ulcer on the patient’s left leg with a raised erythematous border and a base with purulent debris.

9. Similar findings are detected in some macrophages (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400).

1. A 59-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician for trouble sleeping.

1. Patient D is a 50-year-old  female who presents after a motor vehicle collision

1. A 70-year-old woman with long-term tobacco use presented with 2 weeks of bilateral ptosis and binocular horizontal diplopia.

3. On initial examination, she had a normal mental status, no pupillary abnormalities, normal visual acuity, and full visual fields.
4. She had moderate exotropia, severe bilateral ptosis, impaired bilateral adduction and vertical ductions, and impaired convergence.
5. Her abduction and vertical oculocephalic reflexes were intact.
6. She had full strength and normal sensation and reflexes but had a slightly wide-based and unsteady gait.
7. Over the subsequent weeks, she experienced worsening gait, falls, inattention, and short-term memory loss.
8. Her brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast results were unremarkable.
9. The test results for acetylcholine receptor antibodies and the muscle-specific kinase antibody were negative.
10. Her electrodiagnostic test results with repetitive stimulation and single fiber electromyography were unremarkable and there was no evidence of neuropathy.
11. The test results for thyrotropin, thiamine level, Lyme antibodies, rapid plasma reagin, and the serum ganglioside antibody panel were unremarkable.
12. A cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed a nucleated cell count of 6/μL (to convert to ×109 liters, multiply by 0.001) with 88% lymphocytes (to convert to the proportion of 1.0, multiply by 0.01), a red blood cell count of 10/μL, a protein level of 0.087 g/dL (to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10), and glucose level of 63 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555).
13. Serum paraneoplastic antibody testing results were negative for anti-Hu, Ri, Yo, and voltage-gated potassium channel complex (VGKCC) antibodies, and the CSF had negative results for anti-VGKCC, voltage-gated calcium channel, Hu, Ri, Yo, and amphiphysin antibodies.
14. A repeated brain MRI 3 weeks later revealed an interval development of T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities in the right thalamus, inferior temporal gyrus, and hippocampus (Figure).
15. Repeated brain magnetic resonance imaging 3 weeks after the patient’s initial presentation: T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery hyperintensities (arrowheads) in the right inferior temporal gyrus (A) and right thalamus (B).

1. A man in his 60s presented with new-onset bullae and erosions over sun-exposed areas and bony prominences.

8. A, Flaccid bulla and erosions on the left dorsal hand at presentation.  
9. B, Biopsy from the left elbow.

1. Patient D is a 62-year-old  male with history of lung cancer who presents with sudden onset of back pain

7.

1. A 55-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband with a 1 hour history of an unremitting headache.

1. A man in his 30s was referred to the retina clinic with a diagnosis of bilateral branch retinal vein occlusions.  
2. He reported flashes and progressive blurry vision in both eyes over a period of 6 days.  
3. He had no history of eye problems.  
4. His medical history was negative for diabetes and hypertension, and review of systems was positive for recent easy bruising and progressive fatigue.  
5. His initial best-corrected visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS.  
6. Results from examination of his pupils, motility, intraocular pressures, confrontational visual fields, and anterior segments were normal.

8. He had bilateral flame-shaped and intraretinal hemorrhages in both maculae along the superior arcades and some scattered peripheral hemorrhages.  
9. There was no vessel tortuosity, and there were hard exudates in the left macula.

11. Fluorescein angiography of both eyes showed blocking in the areas of hemorrhage, good venous filling, no leakage, and no neovascularization.Wide-field scanning laser image of the left eye showed superficial and intraretinal hemorrhages and hard exudates.

1. A 2-month-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for a follow-up visit.

1. A 56-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of an incidentally discovered adrenal mass.  
2. She experienced no symptoms of weight loss, headache, sweating, palpitations, pallor, anxiety, menstrual abnormalities, or mood changes; had no known history of cancer or hypertension; and was not taking any medications.  
3. On physical examination, her blood pressure was 135/73 mm Hg, and her heart rate was 82/min.

1. A 55-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine physical examination.  
2. He is currently taking no medications.  
3. His pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 165/95 mm Hg.  
4. Physical examination shows no other abnormalities.

1. A school-aged boy experienced generalized erythematous rashes for 4 years.
2. Skin examination showed ichthyosiform brownish plaques on his lower extremities and multiple erythematous confluent papules and plaques on his trunk and face (Figure, A and B).

1. A 65-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because of a 3-day history of severe right-sided flank pain, fever, and vomiting.

1. An 84-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus type 2, hypertension, and a transient ischemic attack 4 years earlier presented to the University of Illinois at Chicago emergency department for evaluation of 1 day of decreased vision in his left eye.

1. Patient D is a 66-year-old  male with history of hepatocellular carcinoma who presents with acute mid back pain

6. You obtain MRI of the thoracic spine, which reveals diffuse osseous metastatic lesions with a severe pathologic fracture at T6
7.

1. Patient D is a 38-year-old  male with a known cervical chordoma status-post multiple resections presenting with 2 months of progressive neck pain accompanied with thoracic and abdominal pain
2. Patient D describes the pain as the worst it has ever been, as it feels like his neck, chest and abdomen are constantly on fire
3. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen provide no relief, and he is now unable to sleep
4. On physical exam, you note dysesthesia to palpation of his neck and pain to deep palpation of his abdomen

6.

1. A 50-year-old man presents to the emergency department with chest pain.
2. He states that the pain is dull in quality, started 30 minutes ago, has been gradually worsening, and is worse with exertion.
3. He also endorses some shortness of breath.
4. He also believes the pain is worse when leaning back and improved when leaning forward.
5. His wife noticed he fainted after the pain started but regained consciousness shortly after.
6. He has a medical history of diabetes and hypertension for which he is on metformin and losartan.
7. His temperature is 99.2°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 130/87 mmHg, pulse is 99/min, respirations are 22/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air.
8. Physical exam reveals an overweight man.
9. A normal S1 and S2 are auscultated with clear breath sounds.
10. An ECG is performed as seen in Figure A.

1. A 75-year-old male presents with a 6-month history of bilateral shoulder pain, more severe on the right side, accompanied by upper arm stiffness and aching.
2. He denies experiencing headache, jaw or arm claudication, scalp tenderness, or double vision.
3. Physical examination reveals normal temperature and equal blood pressure readings of 120/80 mm Hg in both arms.

5. Hip range of motion is normal.
6. Temporal arteries are symmetrical without beading or tenderness, and radial pulses are equal bilaterally.
7. Laboratory testing shows an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 25 mm/hr (normal range: 0-17).

1. A woman in her 50s admitted for bacterial pneumonia was noted to have an ulcerated plaque on the forearm.
2. The patient had been discharged approximately 2 weeks prior, after an admission for congestive heart failure.
3. A few days after that discharge, the patient noticed a painful ulceration on the right distal forearm, at the site where a peripheral intravenous catheter had been inserted during her initial hospitalization.

8. A, An ulcerated plaque on the right forearm.
9. Note 2 tender, 1- to 2-cm red nodules in the right antecubital fossa.
10. B, Dense neutrophilic infiltrate.
11. Note associated tissue necrosis.
12. Hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×20.
13. C, Organisms seen on Gram stain.
14. Original magnification ×60.

1. A 15-month-old boy presents with his mother for his well-child exam.
2. His mother is concerned about his vision, as she noticed him squinting while watching television.
3. The patient was born at 39 weeks of gestation via spontaneous vaginal delivery.
4. He is up to date with routine vaccinations.
5. He is able to walk alone, speak 3 words, and scribble with a crayon.

7. On exam, his pupils are round and reactive to light.
8. A photograph of his eyes is shown in Figure A.
9. When focusing on the pediatrician's penlight, the patient's left eye wanders.

11. The rest of his neurological exam, including extraocular movements, is within normal limits.

1. A 37-year-old G1P0 woman at 37 weeks of gestation presents to the emergency department with complaints of headache and abdominal pain.

3. She has been non-compliant with prenatal care, including medications for her hypertension and diabetes.  
4. The patient is demanding morphine and becomes aggressive when it is denied.  
5. Her vital signs are: temperature 98.2°F (36.8°C), blood pressure 157/105 mm Hg, pulse 82/min, respirations 12/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.  
6. Initial laboratory findings are as follows:  
   - Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL  
   - Hematocrit: 36%  
   - Leukocyte count: 5,500/mm³ with normal differential  
   - Platelet count: 117,000/mm³  
   - Serum:  
     - Na⁺: 141 mEq/L  
     - Cl⁻: 101 mEq/L  
     - K⁺: 5.0 mEq/L  
     - HCO₃⁻: 23 mEq/L  
     - BUN: 29 mg/dL  
     - Glucose: 156 mg/dL

     - Blood: Negative  
   The patient is admitted and treated appropriately, leading to resolution of her symptoms.
